readings.c2s2:
'''2.''' Composed of volunteers: as, a ''volunteer'' corps.

{{smaller block|The ''volunteer'' artillery, furnished by the several States, was only organized into batteries, having no officer above the rank of captain.
{{right|''Comte de Paris'', Civil War in America (trans.), I. 275.}}}}

'''volunteer''' (vol-un-tēr′), ''v.'' [< ''volunteer'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To offer, contribute, or bestow voluntarily, or without constraint or compulsion.

{{smaller block|The chief agents who had already ''volunteered'' their services against him.
{{right|''Gifford'', Note on B. Jonson’s Poetaster, iii. 1.}}
<poem>Bit by bit, the full and true
Particulars of the tale were ''volunteered''
With all the breathless zeal of friendship.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 232.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To enter into any service of one’s free will, without constraint or compulsion: as, to ''volunteer'' for a campaign.

'''volunteerly†''' (vol-un-tēr′li), ''adv.'' Voluntarily; as a volunteer.

{{smaller block|<poem>''Volunteerly'' to ramble with Lord Loudon Campbell,
Brave Ilay did suffer for a’.</poem>
{{right|''Battle of Sheriff-Muir'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 158).}}}}

'''voluntomotory''' (vol″un-tọ̄-mō′tọ̄-ri), ''a.'' [< ''volunt(ary)'' + ''motory''.] Having or pertaining to motor influence or effect which is voluntary, or subject to the will: with Remak specifying the somatopleural division of the body, including the muscular system of ordinary language, as distinguished from the splanchnopleural or ''involuntomotory'' (which see).

{{smaller block|The ''volunto-motory'', corresponding to the body-wall or somatopleure.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VIII. 167.}}}}

¶
'''voluptuously''' (vọ̄-lup′tụ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a voluptuous manner; with free indulgence in sensual pleasures; luxuriously; sensually: as, to live ''voluptuously.''
{{smaller block|''Voluptuously'' surfeit out of action. ''Shak.'', Cor., i. 3. 27.}}

'''voluptuousness''' (vọ̄-lup′tụ̄-us-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being voluptuous, or addicted to the pursuit of pleasure and sensual gratification; luxuriousness.
{{smaller block|<poem>But there ’s no bottom, none,
In my ''voluptuousness;'' your wives, your daughters,
Your matrons, and your maids could not fill up
The cistern of my lust. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 61.</poem>
The ''voluptuousness'' of holding a human being in his [the slave-owner’s] absolute control.
{{right|''Emerson'', West Indian Emancipation.}}
To the north-east, in places, the backs and sides of the mountains have a green, pastoral ''voluptuousness,'' so smooth and full are they with thick turf.
{{right|''The Century'', XXIV. 421.}}}}

'''volupty†''', ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''voluptie;'' < OF. ''volupte'', F. ''volupté'' = Pr. ''voluptat'' = It. ''voluptà, voluttà'', < L. ''volupta(t-)s'', enjoyment, delight.] Voluptuousness. ''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 20.

'''Voluspa''' (vol-us-pä′), ''n.'' [< Icel. ''Völuspā'', the song of the sibyl, < ''völu'', gen. of ''völva'', also ''völfa'' (pl. ''völur''), a prophetess, sibyl, wise woman, + ''spā'', prophesy, also pry, look, > Sc. ''spae:'' see

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|voluntary|6787|Voluspa}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|negative sense of consenting, or not refusing or objecting, in regard to the wish of another.}}
{{smaller block|Some of the pleasantest recollections of my childhood are connected with the ''voluntary'' study of an ancient Bible which belonged to my grandmother.
{{right|''Huxley'', Critiques and Addresses, p. 54.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Spontaneous'' joys, where nature has its play,
The soul adopts, and owns their first-born sway.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 255.}}}}
{{smaller block|He lent a ''willing'' ear to the artful propositions of Sforza.
{{right|''Prescott'', Ferd. and Isa., ii. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''voluntaries'' (-riz). '''1.''' One who engages in any affair of his own choice or free will; a volunteer.
{{smaller block|<poem>Rash, inconsiderate, fiery ''voluntaries'',
With ladies’ faces and fierce dragons’ spleens.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 67.}}}}
Specifically—'''2.''' ''Eccles.'', in Great Britain, one who maintains the doctrine of the mutual independence of the church and the state, and holds that the church should be supported by the voluntary contributions of its members and should be left entirely free to regulate its affairs.—'''3.''' Any work or performance not imposed by another.
{{smaller block|At school he [Wordsworth] wrote some task-verses on subjects imposed by the master, and also some ''voluntaries'' of his own, equally undistinguished by any peculiar merit.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 206.}}}}

'''4.''' In ''church music'', an organ prelude to a service; sometimes, by extension, an interlude or postlude; also, an anthem or other piece of choir-music, especially at the opening of a service. {{smaller|These uses of the word seem to have originated in the fact that such musical exercises are not rubrically prescribed.}}
{{smaller block|The rich may indulge in superfluities. The Ionian muse is somewhat too fond of playing ''voluntaries''.
{{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Virgilius and Horatius.}}}}
{{smaller block|My dear Herr Capellmeister, they say you play the most exquisite ''voluntaries!'' Now do play us one.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iv. 4.}}}}

'''At voluntary†''', voluntarily; by an effort of will.
{{smaller block|Cyrces cuppes were too strong for all antidotes, and womens flatteries too forceable to resist ''at voluntarie''.
{{right|''Greene'', Never Too Late (Works, ed. Dyce, Int., p. xii.).}}}}

'''voluntary†''' (vol′un-tạ̄-ri), ''adv.''   [< ''voluntary'', ''a.'']   Voluntarily.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gold, amber, yvorie, perles, owches, rings,
And all that els was pretious and deare,
The sea unto him ''voluntary'' brings.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. iv. 23.}}}}
{{smaller block|I serve here ''voluntary''.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 1. 103.}}}}

'''voluntaryism''' (vol′un-tạ̄-ri-izm), ''n.''   [< ''voluntary'' + ''-ism''.]   Voluntary principle or action; the system or principle of supporting anything by voluntary contribution or assistance; especially, the principle of unrestricted personal liberty in matters of religion—this involving on the one hand the obligation of church-members to support and maintain religious ordinances, and on the other the church’s entire freedom from state patronage, support, and control.

{{smaller block|Esther . . . was unable at present to give her mind to the original functions of a bishop, or the comparative merits of Endowments and ''Voluntaryism.''
{{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, xli.}}}}

{{smaller block|The transatlantic friend of Vane, at the very nick of time, was the central champion in England of absolute ''voluntaryism'', against the Independents and the famous fifteen proposals for a State Church on their sort of “Christian Fundamentals.”
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXVI. 541.}}}}

{{smaller block|In education, ''voluntaryism'' has been most prominent and most beneficent from early times.
{{right|''Jour. of Education'', XVIII. 148.}}}}

'''voluntaryist''' (vol′un-tā-ri-ist), ''n.''   [< ''voluntary'' + ''-ist.'']   One who believes in or advocates voluntaryism, especially in religion. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|We commend this tribute to the Church of England to our friends on the other side of the water, as proof that an American and a ''Voluntaryist'' can yet do full justice to that ancient and historical church.
{{right|''New York Evangelist'', Oct. 19, 1876.}}}}

'''voluntative''' (vol′un-tā-tiv), ''a.''   [< L. ''voluntа(t-)s'', will, + ''-ive.'']   Voluntary.

{{smaller block|The simple solution seems to be that the conditioning of a purpose destroys its absolute ''voluntative'' power.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', IV. 425.}}}}

'''volunte†''', ''n.'' See ''volunty.''

'''volunteer''' (vol-un-tēr′), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< F. ''volontaire'', now ''volontaire'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''voluntario'', < L. ''voluntarius'', voluntary: see ''voluntary.'']   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A person who enters into any service of his own free will.

{{smaller block|He has had Compassion upon Lovers, and generously engag’d a ''Volunteer'' in this Action, for our Service.
{{right|''Congreve'', Way of the World, v. 14.}}}}

'''2.''' A person who enters military service of his own free will, and not by constraint or compulsion; one who offers to serve, and generally receives some consideration or privileges on that account; in the United States, especially during the civil war, a soldier of a body other than the regular army, but practically governed by the same laws when in service. {{smaller|In Great Britain the government provides the various bodies of volunteers, or citizen-soldiery, with competent instructors, arms, and a part of their ammunition, besides allowing to each corps certain grants proportioned to the number of efficient members, etc. A British volunteer can resign on giving a fortnight’s notice, except in a crisis of imminent danger to the country. In the United States the army of volunteers comprises, to all intents and purposes—(1) the regular unpaid forces of State militia which, when called into the actual service of the United States, receive pay from the government, and are subject to the rules and articles of war, and (2) that class of troops which may from time to time be raised by Congress on occasions of national emergency. Such troops are properly United States troops, and the method of officering them is designated by Congress.}}
{{smaller block|At the very outset of the campaign, the inexperience of the Federal ''volunteers'' was made evident, even more on the march than on the battle-field.
{{right|''Comte de Paris'', Civil War in America (trans.), I. 193.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Volunteers'' often complain that they are not taken seriously enough. . . . Nor must they ever cease complaining until they have been thoroughly organized for whatever their duties are to be, and until those duties are perfectly clear to themselves and the country at large.
{{right|''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 615.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''law'', one who claims the benefit of a contract or conveyance although no consideration proceeded from him nor from any one in whose place he stands.—'''4.''' A tree which grows spontaneously: as, that pear-tree in my garden is a ''volunteer''. [Southern U. S.]

'''II.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Entering into military service by free will and choice: as, a ''volunteer'' soldier.— '''2.''' Composed of volunteers: as, a ''volunteer'' corps.

{{smaller block|The ''volunteer'' artillery, furnished by the several States, was only organized into batteries, having no officer above the rank of captain.
{{right|''Comte de Paris'', Civil War in America (trans.), I. 275.}}}}

'''volunteer''' (vol-un-tēr′), ''v.''   [< ''volunteer'', ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' To offer, contribute, or bestow voluntarily, or without constraint or compulsion.

{{smaller block|The chief agents who had already ''volunteered'' their services against him.
{{right|''Gifford'', Note on B. Jonson’s Poetaster, iii. 1.}}}}
<poem>Bit by bit, the full and true
Particulars of the tale were ''volunteered''
With all the breathless zeal of friendship.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, I. 232.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To enter into any service of one’s free will, without constraint or compulsion: as, to ''volunteer'' for a campaign.

'''volunteerly†''' (vol-un-tēr′li), ''adv.'' Voluntarily; as a volunteer.

<poem>''Volunteerly'' to ramble with Lord Loudon Campbell,
Brave Ilay did suffer for a’.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Battle of Sheriff-Muir'' (Child’s Ballads, VII. 158).}}}}

'''voluntomotory''' (vol″un-tọ̄-mō′tọ̄-ri), ''a.''   [< ''volunt(ary)'' + ''motory''.]   Having or pertaining to motor influence or effect which is voluntary, or subject to the will: with Remak specifying the somatopleural division of the body, including the muscular system of ordinary language, as distinguished from the splanchnopleural or ''involuntomotory'' (which see).

{{smaller block|The ''volunto-motory'', corresponding to the body-wall or somatopleure.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', VIII. 167.}}}}

'''volunty†''', ''n.''   [< ME. ''volunte'', also ''volente'', ''voulente'', < OF. ''volente'', ''volunte'', F. ''volonté'' = Sp. ''voluntad'' = It. ''volontà'', will, < L. ''volunta(t-)s'', will, desire: see ''voluntary''.]   Will; wish; will and pleasure.
{{smaller block|<poem>For that he
May not fulfille his ''volunte''.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of the Rose'', l. 5276.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For of free choice and hertely ''volente'',
She hathe to God avowed chastité.</poem>
{{right|''Lydgate'', MS. Ashmole 339, f. 15. (''Halliwell.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>After me made by thy will and ''uolente''
To take this woman of the fayry,
This here diffamed serpent vnto se.</poem>
{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3473.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Sir,” quod thei, “yef it be not thus, doth with vs youre ''volente.''” {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 29.}}}}
{{smaller block|And the seid Tuddenham and Heydon wold after theyr ''voulente'' have it hald yn meen of the maner of Hetersete, whych sufficient evidenses that ye have specifyeth no thyng soo. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 173.}}}}

'''voluper†''', ''n.''   [ME., also ''volupeer'', ''voleper''.]   A cap or head-dress worn in the fourteenth century by either sex.
{{smaller block|<poem>The tapes of hir white ''voluper''
Were of the same suyte of hir coler.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 55.}}}}

'''voluptie†''', ''n.'' See ''volupty''.

'''voluptuary''' (vō-lup′t̮ū-ā-ri), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [= F. ''voluptuaire'' = It. ''voluttuario'', < L. ''voluptuarius'', for earlier ''voluptarius'', of or pertaining to pleasure, < ''volupta(t-)s'', enjoyment, delight: see ''volupty''.]'' '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Pertaining or contributing to luxury and sensual pleasure; promoting sensual indulgence.
{{smaller block|The arts which flourish in times while virtue is in growth are military, and while virtue is in state are liberal, and while virtue is in declination are ''voluptuary.''
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The works of the ''voluptuary'' arts are properly attributed to Vulcan, the God of Fire.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii., Expl.}}}}
'''2.''' Given to sensual indulgence; voluptuous: as, ''voluptuary'' habits.

'''II.''' ''n.''; pl. ''voluptuaries'' (-riz). A man given up to luxury or the gratification of the appetite and other sensual indulgences; a sensualist.
{{smaller block|Does not the ''voluptuary'' understand, in all the liberties of a loose and lewd conversation, that he runs the risk of body and soul?
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The parable was intended against the ''voluptuaries'' of that time, . . . men who, notwithstanding they professed themselves Jews, lived like Heathens.
{{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. xii.}}}}
{{smaller block|We have the ''Voluptuary'', when first pleasant feelings, and secondly the pleasantness of pleasant feelings, are made the end to which all else is means, and the abstraction of pleasure’s sake is pursued.
{{right|''F. H. Bradley'', Ethical Studies, p. 253, note.}}}}

'''voluptuate†''' (vō-lup′t̮ū-āt), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''voluptu''(''ous'') + ''-ate''<sup>2</sup>.]   To make luxurious or delightful.
{{smaller block|’Tis watching and labour that ''voluptuates'' repose and sleep.
{{right|''Feltham'', Resolves, ii. 44.}}}}

'''voluptuosity†''' (vō-lup-t̮ū-os′i̤-ti), ''n.''   [< ''voluptuous'' + ''-ity.'']   Voluptuousness.

{{smaller block|In some children nature is more prone to vice than to vertue, and in the tender wittes be sparkes of ''voluptuositie.''
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, i. 6.}}}}

'''voluptuous''' (vō-lup′t̮ū-us), ''a.''   [< ME. ''voluptuous'', < OF. *''voluptuous'', F. ''voluptueux'' = Sp. Pg. ''voluptuoso'' = It. ''voluttuoso'', < L. ''voluptuosus'', full of gratification, delightful, < ''volupta(t-)s'', pleasure: see ''volupty''.]   '''1.''' Pertaining to, proceeding from, or inclined to sensual gratification: as, ''voluptuous'' tastes or habits.—'''2.''' Passed or spent in luxury or sensuality.
{{smaller block|Soften’d with pleasure and ''voluptuous'' life.
{{right|''Milton'', S. A., l. 534.}}}}
'''3.''' Contributing to sensual pleasure; exciting, or tending to excite, sensual desires and indulgence; sensual.
{{smaller block|He that is temperate fleeth pleasures ''voluptuous.''
{{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 20.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Voluptuous'' idleness. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xix. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Ah, Vice! how soft are thy ''voluptuous'' ways!
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, i. 65.}}}}
{{smaller block|Barbara Palmer, Duchess of Cleveland, was there, no longer young, but still retaining some traces of that superb and ''voluptuous'' loveliness which twenty years before overcame the hearts of all men. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|The face ''voluptuous'', yet pure; funeste, but innocent.
{{right|''J. S. Fanu'', Tenants of Mallory, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Low ''voluptuous'' music winding.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Vision of Sin, ii.}}}}
'''4.''' Given to the enjoyments of luxury and pleasure; indulging in sensual gratifications.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou wilt bring me soon
. . . where I shall reign
At thy right hand ''voluptuous'', as beseems
Thy daughter and thy darling, without end.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 869.}}}}
{{smaller block|Jolly and ''voluptuous'' livers.
{{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, IV. iv.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Carnal, Sensuous'', etc. See ''sensual.''

'''voluptuously''' (vọ̄-lup′tụ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a voluptuous manner; with free indulgence in sensual pleasures; luxuriously; sensually: as, to live ''voluptuously.''
{{smaller block|''Voluptuously'' surfeit out of action.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 3. 27.}}}}

'''voluptuousness''' (vọ̄-lup′tụ̄-us-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being voluptuous, or addicted to the pursuit of pleasure and sensual gratification; luxuriousness.
{{smaller block|<poem>But there ’s no bottom, none,
In my ''voluptuousness;'' your wives, your daughters,
Your matrons, and your maids could not fill up
The cistern of my lust. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 3. 61.</poem>
The ''voluptuousness'' of holding a human being in his [the slave-owner’s] absolute control.
{{right|''Emerson'', West Indian Emancipation.}}}}
{{smaller block|To the north-east, in places, the backs and sides of the mountains have a green, pastoral ''voluptuousness,'' so smooth and full are they with thick turf.
{{right|''The Century'', XXIV. 421.}}}}

'''volupty†''', ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''voluptie;'' < OF. ''volupte'', F. ''volupté'' = Pr. ''voluptat'' = It. ''voluptà, voluttà'', < L. ''volupta(t-)s'', enjoyment, delight.]   Voluptuousness.   ''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 20.

'''Voluspa''' (vol-us-pä′), ''n.''   [< Icel. ''Völuspā'', the song of the sibyl, < ''völu'', gen. of ''völva'', also ''völfa'' (pl. ''völur''), a prophetess, sibyl, wise woman, + ''spā'', prophesy, also pry, look, > Sc. ''spae:'' see<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
